title: Enterprise AI Agents — CRM & Customer Support (Agentforce, Breeze, Fin, Zendesk)

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Lesson 16-10 was about using general-purpose AI tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity) to help *you* do sales work — research, outreach, proposals. This lesson is different: it's about the AI agents that are increasingly *built directly into* the CRM and customer-support software your company already pays for — Salesforce, HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Zendesk, and Intercom (now rebranded Fin).

These aren't chatbots you paste text into. They're agents with permission to take real actions inside your systems of record: updating a lead's status, drafting and sending a reply, closing a support ticket, escalating a case. By the end of this lesson you'll know what each major platform offers, how to tell what your own company already has access to, and — because these agents act rather than just draft — why the governance question matters more here than almost anywhere else in this course.

## Salesforce Agentforce

Agentforce is Salesforce's autonomous agent layer, built on top of the core CRM data your company already stores in Salesforce. It can triage incoming cases, qualify and route leads, answer customer questions using your company's own knowledge base, and take actions on CRM records — updating fields, logging activities, escalating to a human — all with configurable guardrails rather than free-for-all autonomy.

**It's no longer a demo — it's a real revenue line.** Agentforce reported roughly **$1.2 billion in annual recurring revenue** in its most recent reported quarter, up over 200% year-over-year, meaning a large number of real companies have this switched on in production today, not just piloting it.

**A detail worth knowing:** Salesforce and Anthropic have a deep partnership — Claude is a foundational model inside Agentforce and Salesforce's broader platform, with Salesforce keeping Claude traffic inside its own trust boundary for regulated customers. So the same model family you've been using throughout this course to draft emails and write code may also be the one quietly triaging a support case at your company. (Salesforce also offers OpenAI's models as an alternative inside Agentforce — it's a multi-model platform, not an exclusive one.)

**Governance layer:** Salesforce's **Einstein Trust Layer** sits underneath Agentforce specifically to handle data governance — masking sensitive data before it reaches a model, keeping an audit trail of what the agent saw and did, and enforcing the same permission sets and sharing rules a human user would be bound by. This is the piece to ask about if your company is evaluating Agentforce: guardrails are configurable, not automatic.

## HubSpot Breeze, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and the Rest of the CRM Field

**HubSpot Breeze** is HubSpot's answer to the same idea, split into three pieces: **Breeze Assistant** (in-line AI help while you work), **Breeze Agents** (autonomous agents that can draft outreach, qualify inbound leads, and update CRM records without a human doing the data entry), and **Breeze Studio** (where admins configure and customize agent behavior for their own business). If your company runs its sales and marketing on HubSpot rather than Salesforce, this is the equivalent capability to check for.

**Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales Copilot** (increasingly marketed under the broader "Copilot" and "Copilot Cowork" branding) brings the same category of capability into Dynamics 365 — surfacing next-best-action suggestions, drafting customer emails and meeting summaries, and, in its more agentic modes, taking actions on records directly. If your organisation is a Microsoft shop already licensing Copilot for Microsoft 365, there's a good chance a Dynamics-side agent layer is included or available as an add-on.

**The pattern across all three:** the AI agent isn't a separate product you have to go buy and integrate — it's a layer that sits on top of data you've already been entering into your CRM for years. That's exactly why the next section on evaluating what you already have matters so much.

## Customer Support: Intercom Fin and Zendesk AI Agents

On the support side, two products are worth knowing by name because they now resolve a majority of support volume without a human touching the ticket:

**Intercom Fin** (Intercom rebranded itself as simply **Fin** as it narrowed its focus to AI customer-service agents) resolves customer queries end-to-end across chat, email, WhatsApp, SMS, phone, and Slack, using its own purpose-built model, Apex. Fin's reported resolution rate — cases closed without human involvement — runs around **76% of support volume** across those channels. This got serious enough that **Salesforce announced it is acquiring Fin for roughly $3.6 billion** in mid-2026, specifically to bolt Fin's fast-to-deploy, pre-trained agent onto Agentforce for customers who don't want (or can't afford the time for) heavy customization — Salesforce's largest acquisition since Slack.

**Zendesk AI Agents** offer the equivalent inside Zendesk's support platform: automated ticket resolution, sentiment-aware escalation to a human agent when a case is outside the AI's confidence threshold, and resolution-rate dashboards that support leaders now track as a core operating metric, the same way they'd track average handle time or CSAT.

**Why this matters practically:** if your company runs support through Zendesk or Intercom/Fin, there is very likely an AI agent tier already available on your plan or as an upgrade — support leaders today are expected to know their AI resolution rate the way they know their CSAT score.

**The practical framing for this lesson:** if your company already uses Salesforce, HubSpot, Dynamics 365, Zendesk, or Intercom/Fin, there is a real chance an AI agent layer is already licensed and simply switched off, or available as a one-click add-on you've never asked about. This lesson is about *recognizing and evaluating* what's already there — not about building something from scratch the way earlier Part 16 lessons were.

**These agents take real actions — treat them with more scrutiny than a drafting tool.** A chatbot that only drafts an email you still have to send is low-risk if it gets something wrong; you catch it before it goes out. An agent that closes a support ticket, updates a CRM record, or reassigns a lead has already acted by the time anyone reviews it. Before your team turns on autonomous actions (not just autonomous drafting) in any of these platforms, confirm: is there an audit trail of what the agent changed and why? Is there a human-review or escalation path for edge cases? Can a manager see resolution/action logs, not just a summary? Governance here isn't optional paperwork — it's the difference between a helpful agent and a support ticket closed incorrectly with no one noticing for weeks.

sections.title: Audit What's Already Available to You
sections.content:
Not everyone reading this has admin access to an enterprise CRM or support platform — this workshop is designed to work either way. Your goal is a real, one-page "what's already available to me" audit you could actually bring to a manager or team meeting.

**Step 1 — Identify your platform(s).** What does your company (or a company you're familiar with — a past employer, a client, a friend's business) actually use for CRM and/or customer support? Salesforce, HubSpot, Dynamics 365, Zendesk, Intercom/Fin, or something else entirely?

**Step 2 — Investigate what AI agent capability exists on your plan.** If you have login access: look in admin settings for "Agentforce," "Breeze," "Copilot," "AI Agents," or similar — most platforms surface a setup or trial toggle even if it isn't turned on. If you don't have admin access: search "[your platform name] AI agent pricing" and read the vendor's own plan-comparison page, or ask whoever manages the platform at your company what tier you're on.

**Step 3 — Write your one-page audit** with these sections:
- **Platform(s) in use:** name and current plan/tier
- **AI agent features already licensed:** what's switched on right now, if anything
- **AI agent features available as an add-on:** what exists on your platform but isn't enabled, and roughly what it would cost or require to turn on
- **One concrete use case:** a specific, recurring task at your company (or the company you researched) this could plausibly help with — e.g. "first-response drafting for the 40 support tickets we get most weekday mornings" — not a vague "AI could help with support"
- **One governance question you'd want answered before flipping it on:** referencing the audit-trail/escalation-path concerns from this lesson

**Step 4 — Save this document somewhere you'll actually find it again**, and if it's genuinely relevant, share it with whoever owns the CRM/support platform decision at your organisation. This is the kind of one-page brief that gets a 15-minute conversation started — which is the real point of the exercise.

sections.question: Your company's support team uses Zendesk and is considering turning on Zendesk's AI Agents to auto-resolve simple tickets. A team member says, 'Great, let's turn on full autonomous resolution for everything so we can cut our ticket backlog fastest.' What's the most important thing to check before doing that?
options: Nothing — AI agents at major vendors are pre-configured to be safe by default, so full autonomy is fine to enable immediately

Whether there's an escalation path for tickets outside the AI's confidence threshold, an audit trail of resolved tickets, and a way for a human to review resolution quality — not just the resolution-rate number
Only the monthly cost of the AI Agents add-on
Whether the AI Agents feature uses the same underlying model as Agentforce
sections.explanation: Resolution rate alone is a vanity metric if you can't see *what* got resolved and *how*. Because these agents take real action — closing tickets, not just drafting replies — the safety net is the escalation path (for ambiguous or high-stakes cases) and the audit trail (so a manager can spot a pattern of incorrectly closed tickets before it damages customer trust, not months later). Cost (C) matters but isn't the most important gate before enabling autonomous *action*. Which model powers it (D) is interesting context but not the operational safeguard that matters here.

sections.question: A sales manager wants to know if their company's HubSpot subscription already includes AI agent capability like autonomous lead qualification and record updates, or if it would require an upgrade. What's the most reliable first step?
options: Assume it's included, since most modern CRM software has this built in by default

Check the admin settings for Breeze Agents / Breeze Studio in their HubSpot account, or check HubSpot's current plan-comparison page against their subscription tier, or ask whoever manages the HubSpot contract at the company
Wait for HubSpot to send an email announcing the feature
Assume it's not included, since AI agent features are always a separate paid product
sections.explanation: Neither blanket assumption (A or D) is reliable — AI agent tiers vary a lot by vendor, by plan level, and change frequently as vendors bundle or unbundle features. The reliable path is checking directly: admin settings often expose a setup flow even for unenabled features, and the vendor's own plan-comparison page (or whoever owns the contract) will have the current, accurate answer. This is exactly the audit habit this lesson's workshop is meant to build.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 16-12.** You now know the major enterprise AI agent products built into the CRM and support tools millions of office workers already use — Salesforce Agentforce, HubSpot Breeze, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales Copilot, Intercom Fin, and Zendesk AI Agents — what each does, roughly how big and real this market already is, and why governance (audit trails, escalation paths, human review) matters more once an agent can act on a record instead of just drafting text. You've also produced a real audit of what's available to you or your organisation today.
